blocks.body:
In ordinary arithmetic you solve $11x = 5$ by dividing by $11$. Can you solve $11x \equiv 5 \pmod{26}$ the same way? You can, provided you find a number that behaves like $\frac{1}{11}$ modulo $26$, that is, a number $u$ with $11u \equiv 1 \pmod{26}$. Then multiplying by $u$ undoes multiplication by $11$.

Such a $u$ is called an inverse. This lesson answers when inverses exist (exactly when the number is coprime to the modulus), how to compute them quickly with the extended Euclidean algorithm, and how to solve every linear congruence $ax \equiv b \pmod n$, including the cases where division is impossible.

blocks.title: Modular inverse
blocks.body:
Let $n \ge 1$. An integer $u$ is an inverse of $a$ modulo $n$ if
$$au \equiv 1 \pmod n.$$
When it exists it is unique modulo $n$ and is written $a^{-1} \bmod n$. An integer that has an inverse modulo $n$ is called a unit modulo $n$.

An inverse is the residue that undoes multiplication by $a$.

blocks.title: Who has an inverse?
blocks.body:
Try small cases. Modulo $7$ every non-zero residue has an inverse:
$$1 \cdot 1 \equiv 1, \quad 2 \cdot 4 = 8 \equiv 1, \quad 3 \cdot 5 = 15 \equiv 1, \quad 6 \cdot 6 = 36 \equiv 1 \pmod 7.$$
Modulo $10$ only $1, 3, 7, 9$ have inverses ($3 \cdot 7 = 21$, $9 \cdot 9 = 81$). The residue $2$ cannot have one: $2u$ is even, and an even number minus $1$ is odd, so it is never a multiple of $10$. The same argument, using the common factor $2$ or $5$ in place of $2$, rules out $4, 5, 6, 8$ and $0$. The pattern is that the units are exactly the residues sharing no factor with the modulus.

blocks.title: Existence of inverses
blocks.body:
Let $n \ge 1$ and let $a$ be an integer. Then
$$a x \equiv 1 \pmod n \text{ has a solution} \iff \gcd(a,n) = 1,$$
and in that case the solution is unique modulo $n$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
If $ax \equiv 1 \pmod n$, then $ax - 1 = ny$ for some integer $y$, so $ax - ny = 1$. Any common divisor of $a$ and $n$ divides the left-hand side, hence divides $1$; so $\gcd(a, n) = 1$.

Conversely, if $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, Bézout's identity ([[bezout]]) gives integers $x, y$ with $ax + ny = 1$. Reducing modulo $n$ gives $ax \equiv 1$.

Uniqueness: if $ax \equiv 1$ and $ax' \equiv 1$, then
$$x \equiv x \cdot (ax') = (xa) \cdot x' \equiv x' \pmod n.$$

blocks.title: Computing inverses
blocks.body:
The proof is also the algorithm: the coefficient of $a$ in a Bézout relation $ax + ny = 1$ is the inverse. For example, to invert $17$ modulo $43$:
$$\begin{aligned} 43 &= 2 \cdot 17 + 9 \\ 17 &= 1 \cdot 9 + 8 \\ 9 &= 1 \cdot 8 + 1 \end{aligned}$$
and backwards,
$$1 = 9 - 8 = 9 - (17 - 9) = 2 \cdot 9 - 17 = 2(43 - 2\cdot 17) - 17 = 2 \cdot 43 - 5 \cdot 17.$$
So $17 \cdot (-5) \equiv 1 \pmod{43}$, and $17^{-1} \equiv -5 \equiv 38 \pmod{43}$. Check: $17 \cdot 38 = 646 = 15 \cdot 43 + 1$.

This takes a number of steps proportional to the number of digits, so inverses modulo numbers with hundreds of digits are computed instantly. That speed is what makes modular inverses usable in cryptography. (In Python, pow(a, -1, n) does exactly this.)

When the modulus is a prime $p$, every residue not divisible by $p$ is coprime to $p$ and so has an inverse. In other words, in $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ you can divide by anything non-zero: it is a field, just like the rationals. This is one of the main reasons primes are pleasant moduli. One small fact worth knowing: modulo a prime, the only residues equal to their own inverse are $\pm 1$, since $x^2 \equiv 1$ means $p \mid (x-1)(x+1)$, and a prime dividing a product divides one of the factors.

blocks.title: Linear congruences
blocks.body:
Let $n \ge 1$, let $a, b$ be integers and $g = \gcd(a, n)$. The congruence
$$ax \equiv b \pmod n$$
has a solution if and only if $g \mid b$. In that case it has exactly $g$ solutions modulo $n$: if $x_0$ is one of them, the solutions are
$$x \equiv x_0 + k\,\frac{n}{g} \pmod n, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, g - 1.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
The congruence holds exactly when $ax - b = ny$ for some integer $y$, that is, when $ax - ny = b$ is solvable. By Bézout's identity the values of $ax - ny$ are precisely the multiples of $g$, so a solution exists if and only if $g \mid b$.

Suppose $g \mid b$. Then $n \mid ax - b$ if and only if $\frac{n}{g} \mid \frac{a}{g}x - \frac{b}{g}$, so the congruence is equivalent to
$$\frac{a}{g}\, x \equiv \frac{b}{g} \pmod{\frac{n}{g}}.$$
The numbers $a/g$ and $n/g$ are coprime (dividing a Bézout relation $ax' + ny' = g$ by $g$ gives a combination equal to $1$). So $a/g$ has an inverse modulo $n/g$, and the reduced congruence has a unique solution $x \equiv x_0 \pmod{n/g}$.

It remains to count these modulo $n$. The integers congruent to $x_0$ modulo $n/g$ are $x_0 + k\frac{n}{g}$ for $k \in \mathbb Z$, and two of them are congruent modulo $n$ exactly when their values of $k$ are congruent modulo $g$. So $k = 0, 1, \dots, g-1$ gives each solution modulo $n$ exactly once.

blocks.title: A unique solution
blocks.solution:
Since $\gcd(11, 26) = 1$ there is exactly one solution modulo $26$. Find $11^{-1}$:
$$26 = 2 \cdot 11 + 4, \qquad 11 = 2 \cdot 4 + 3, \qquad 4 = 1 \cdot 3 + 1,$$
$$1 = 4 - 3 = 4 - (11 - 2 \cdot 4) = 3 \cdot 4 - 11 = 3(26 - 2 \cdot 11) - 11 = 3 \cdot 26 - 7 \cdot 11.$$
So $11^{-1} \equiv -7 \equiv 19 \pmod{26}$ (check: $11 \cdot 19 = 209 = 8 \cdot 26 + 1$). Multiply the congruence by $19$:
$$x \equiv 19 \cdot 5 = 95 \equiv 17 \pmod{26}.$$
Check: $11 \cdot 17 = 187 = 7 \cdot 26 + 5$.

blocks.title: Several solutions, or none
blocks.body: Solve $12x \equiv 18 \pmod{30}$, and show that $12x \equiv 20 \pmod{30}$ has no solution.
blocks.solution:
Here $g = \gcd(12, 30) = 6$ and $6 \mid 18$, so there are $6$ solutions modulo $30$. Divide everything, including the modulus, by $6$:
$$2x \equiv 3 \pmod 5.$$
The inverse of $2$ modulo $5$ is $3$, so $x \equiv 9 \equiv 4 \pmod 5$. Modulo $30$ the solutions are
$$x \equiv 4,\ 9,\ 14,\ 19,\ 24,\ 29 \pmod{30}.$$
For instance $12 \cdot 9 = 108 = 3 \cdot 30 + 18$.

For $12x \equiv 20$: since $6 \nmid 20$ there is no solution. Directly, $12x - 30y$ is always a multiple of $6$ and $20$ is not.

blocks.title: Multiplying by a unit shuffles the residues
blocks.body: Let $\gcd(a, n) = 1$. Show that $a \cdot 1, a \cdot 2, \dots, a \cdot n$ leave all $n$ possible remainders on division by $n$, each exactly once. Use this to find which of $7, 14, 21, \dots, 70$ ends in the digit $3$.
blocks.solution:
If $ai \equiv aj \pmod n$, multiply by $a^{-1}$ to get $i \equiv j \pmod n$. For $1 \le i, j \le n$ this forces $i = j$. So the $n$ numbers $a, 2a, \dots, na$ lie in $n$ different residue classes, which means they hit every class once.

For the second part, $\gcd(7, 10) = 1$, so exactly one of $7k$ with $1 \le k \le 10$ is $\equiv 3 \pmod{10}$. To find it, solve $7k \equiv 3 \pmod{10}$: since $7 \cdot 3 = 21 \equiv 1$, the inverse of $7$ is $3$, and $k \equiv 9$. The number is $63$.

This "multiplication by a unit permutes the residues" fact is the key step in the proof of [[fermat-euler|Fermat's little theorem]].

blocks.title: A harmonic sum modulo p
blocks.body: Let $p$ be an odd prime and write $1 + \frac12 + \frac13 + \cdots + \frac{1}{p-1} = \frac{A}{B}$ in lowest terms. Prove that $p \mid A$.
blocks.solution:
Put everything over the common denominator $(p-1)!$:
$$1 + \frac12 + \cdots + \frac{1}{p-1} = \frac{N}{(p-1)!}, \qquad N = \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{(p-1)!}{k}.$$
Each $\frac{(p-1)!}{k}$ is an integer, and $k \cdot \frac{(p-1)!}{k} = (p-1)!$. Multiplying by $k^{-1}$ modulo $p$ gives $\frac{(p-1)!}{k} \equiv (p-1)! \cdot k^{-1} \pmod p$. Hence
$$N \equiv (p-1)! \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} k^{-1} \pmod p.$$
As $k$ runs over $1, \dots, p-1$, so does $k^{-1}$ (in some order), because inversion is a bijection on the non-zero residues: applying it twice gives back the residue you started with. So
$$\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} k^{-1} \equiv \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} k = \frac{p(p-1)}{2} \equiv 0 \pmod p,$$
using that $p$ is odd so $\frac{p-1}{2}$ is an integer. Thus $p \mid N$.

Finally $\frac{A}{B}$ is $\frac{N}{(p-1)!}$ reduced. The prime $p$ does not divide $(p-1)!$, so it does not divide $\gcd(N, (p-1)!)$, and it survives in $A = N/\gcd(N, (p-1)!)$. For $p = 5$: $1 + \frac12 + \frac13 + \frac14 = \frac{25}{12}$. In fact Wolstenholme proved that $p^2 \mid A$ for every prime $p \ge 5$, as $25$ illustrates.

blocks.body:
- $a^{-1} \bmod n$ is an integer residue, not the fraction $1/a$. The inverse of $2$ modulo $7$ is $4$.
- The inverse depends on the modulus: $3^{-1} \equiv 5 \pmod 7$ but $3^{-1} \equiv 7 \pmod{10}$.
- When reducing $ax \equiv b \pmod n$ by $g$, divide the modulus too. Dividing $12x \equiv 18 \pmod{30}$ only on the left and right gives $2x \equiv 3 \pmod{30}$, which has no solutions at all (the left side is even, the right odd, and $30$ is even).
- A linear congruence with $g > 1$ has $g$ solutions modulo $n$, not one. Saying "$x \equiv 4 \pmod 5$" is correct; saying "$x \equiv 4 \pmod{30}$" loses five solutions.
- Units modulo composite $n$ can have square roots of $1$ other than $\pm 1$: $4^2 = 16 \equiv 1 \pmod{15}$.

Inverses are the ingredient in the [[crt]], whose solution formula needs the inverse of one modulus modulo another. Pairing each residue with its inverse modulo $p$ proves [[wilson]], and lifting solutions from $p$ to $p^k$ in [[hensel]] uses an inverse at each step.

In [[rsa]], the private exponent is a single modular inverse, $d \equiv e^{-1} \pmod{\varphi(n)}$, computed by exactly the extended Euclidean algorithm above. There is also a second way to invert modulo a prime: by [[fermat-euler]], $a^{p-1} \equiv 1$ when $p \nmid a$, so then $a^{-1} \equiv a^{p-2} \pmod p$.

The units modulo $n$ form a group under multiplication, written $(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times$, and much of the later theory is about the structure of this group; see [[groups]] and [[order-primroot]].

1. Find the inverse of $7$ modulo $31$.
2. Solve $9x \equiv 6 \pmod{15}$, listing all solutions modulo $15$.
3. List the units modulo $12$ and the inverse of each. What do you notice?
4. For which $b$ is $10x \equiv b \pmod{35}$ solvable, and how many solutions does it then have modulo $35$?
